Translate
trans-LATE
verb
From the Latin translatus, “carried across” (past participle of transferre, “to carry over”); hence to bear across, to transfer, to remove from one place or state to another. The narrowing to the rendering of words from one tongue to another is a later and lesser sense.

Biblical Definition

To translate, in the Authorized Version, is to carry across — to transfer, to remove bodily from one place or state to another. The modern reader thinks first of turning words from one language into another, but that is a late and narrow use; the KJV’s translate is a verb of removal, a bearing-over of persons and kingdoms. Abner swears to translate the kingdom “from the house of Saul” and to set up David’s throne (2Sa 3:10) — to carry the crown across from one house to another. Enoch was translated bodily out of this life: “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him” (Heb 11:5) — caught away, removed, borne across the river of death without passing through it. But the word’s glory is in Paul’s gospel, where it describes what God has done to every believer: He “hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son” (Col 1:13). Mark the two kingdoms and the carrying-over between them. The Christian has not been coaxed to change sides; he has been seized out of the dominion of darkness and transferred, a whole man, into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love. This is the language of that other word to Paul — “to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18). Regeneration is a translation. The sinner does not migrate by degrees; he is carried across in a moment by sovereign grace, from death to life, from Satan’s realm to Christ’s.

Webster 1828 Definition

To carry across; to transfer; to remove from one place or state to another — not merely to render into another tongue.

TRANSLATE, to bear across; to remove or transfer from one place or condition to another.

From Latin transferre, “to carry over,” participle translatus.

The sense of rendering words from one language to another is a later narrowing.

Enoch was translated that he should not see death (Heb 11:5).

God hath translated believers into the kingdom of His Son (Col 1:13).

Key Scripture

Col 1:13 — "Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son:"

Heb 11:5 — "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God."

2Sa 3:10 — "To translate the kingdom from the house of Saul, and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba."

Act 26:18 — "To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me."

Modern Corruption

An old word for carrying across; it recovers regeneration as a translation out of darkness into the kingdom of the Son.

expand to see more

The drift here is a narrowing rather than a reversal, but it is real. Our first thought at “translate” is of language — the rendering of a text from Greek into English — and that sense, though good, is small beside the KJV’s. There translate is to carry a thing bodily across: a crown from Saul’s house to David’s, Enoch out of life without dying, a sinner from one kingdom into another. A reader who hears only the linguistic sense will miss the sheer physical force of Col 1:13, where God does not merely teach or persuade the sinner but lifts and carries him out of the domain of darkness altogether.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the monergism of the new birth. To be saved is to be translated — carried across — and the verb has no room for the sinner’s own legs. God “hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son”: the deliverance and the translation are His act, done to a man who was under the power of darkness and could not walk himself out. Regeneration is not a decision that migrates a man by inches but a sovereign removal that bears him over in a moment, from death to life, from Satan’s realm to Christ’s. As Enoch was not found because God had taken him, so the believer is not found in the old kingdom, because God has carried him into the new.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to carry across, to transfer, to remove from one state to another.

expand to see more

Translate — Latin transferre, “to carry over.”

From trans (“across”) + latus, “carried.”

In the KJV it means to transfer or remove, not chiefly to render words.

Enoch was translated that he should not see death (Heb 11:5).

God translated believers into the kingdom of His Son (Col 1:13).

Usage

"To translate in the KJV is to carry across: God “translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son.”"

"Enoch was translated that he should not see death — borne over without dying."

"Abner would translate the kingdom from Saul’s house to David’s throne."
